templates.text: The auditory pathway is among the first to myelinate, allowing the newborn to begin processing the complex acoustic world.
Early myelination of the auditory nerve provides a foundation for orienting to the mother's voice within the first days.
Priority myelination of the auditory tract sharpens the infant's startle response to sudden, loud sounds.
The cochlear nerve and its central auditory projections show leading myelination, priming the system for sound localization.
Myelination advances rapidly along the auditory brainstem pathways, reducing neural transmission delay to just {milliseconds} ms.
This infant's early auditory myelination supports a clear, vigorous cry with well-modulated acoustic features.
The superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus show preferential myelination, enhancing binaural auditory processing.
Leading auditory pathway myelination underpins the infant's ability to quiet to a soft, rhythmic voice.
Early wrapping of the auditory nerve fibers facilitates a more consistent head turn toward a sound source.
The infant's auditory cortex receives myelinated input earlier than some visual areas, prioritizing sound over sight.
Myelination of the auditory radiations is ahead of schedule, supporting rapid habituation to repeated noises.
This advanced auditory tract myelination may correlate with a lower auditory threshold, noticing sounds as quiet as {decibels} dB.
The brainstem's auditory reflex arcs are myelinating early, enabling swift, protective responses to acoustic stimuli.
Priority given to the auditory pathway myelination helps the newborn distinguish prosodic contours in human speech.
Early insulation of the cochlear nucleus axons accelerates the relay of sound information to higher centers.
The infant's auditory system benefits from leading myelination, which refines the Moro reflex trigger to specific sound qualities.
Myelination is actively sheathing the inferior colliculus pathways, crucial for orienting to novel auditory events.
This preferential auditory myelination lays the groundwork for early vocal turn-taking and communication.
The medial geniculate body shows early myelination, acting as a thalamic relay primed for auditory signals.
Leading auditory nerve myelination contributes to a more organized sleep-wake cycle in response to sound cues.
Early myelination along the auditory pathway supports the infant's ability to synchronize movement to rhythmic sounds.
The acoustic striae are among the first white matter tracts to myelinate, enhancing sound processing speed.
Priority auditory myelination may manifest as a shorter latency, under {seconds} second, in the auditory blink reflex.
Myelination is advancing briskly in the auditory cortex's subplate, preparing for complex sound discrimination.
The infant's early auditory pathway development is marked by robust myelination of the trapezoid body fibers.
This leading auditory myelination facilitates a clearer differentiation between the infant's own cry and other sounds.
Myelination prioritizes the auditory system, allowing the newborn to use sound as a primary organizer of state and attention.
The eighth cranial nerve's central processes are sheathing early, providing a high-fidelity conduit for auditory information.
Early auditory tract myelination underpins the infant's capacity for consoling by voice within the first week.
Myelination is selectively advancing in auditory projection fibers, fine-tuning the brain's response to frequency and intensity.
